passages.body: Cities are consistently warmer than the countryside around them, a phenomenon researchers call the urban heat island effect. The cause is largely structural: asphalt and concrete absorb solar radiation during the day and release it slowly after dark, while the vertical surfaces of tall buildings trap heat that would otherwise escape upward. Vegetation, which cools the air through evaporation, is scarce in dense districts. The result is a temperature gap that can reach five degrees Celsius on a still summer night. For much of the twentieth century this was treated as a curiosity rather than a problem. That changed as heat waves grew more frequent and their death tolls became harder to ignore. Studies of the 2003 European heat wave found that urban residents died at markedly higher rates than rural ones, and that the difference persisted even after accounting for age and income. Municipal responses have tended toward the visible: planting trees, painting roofs white, adding parks. These measures work, but their effect is local and modest. A white roof cools the building beneath it far more than the street outside. Some researchers argue that meaningful change requires rethinking how cities are zoned and built, a far slower and more contentious undertaking than planting a row of trees.

Before the railways, time in Britain was a local matter. Each town set its clocks by the sun, so noon in Bristol fell roughly ten minutes after noon in London. For most purposes the discrepancy was invisible; a farmer had no reason to care what hour it was two hundred miles away. Railway timetables made the difference impossible to ignore. A train leaving London at nine and arriving in Bristol at eleven was, by Bristol's clocks, arriving at ten fifty. Companies began publishing schedules in London time and instructing stations to adopt it, a practice that spread along the lines themselves. By 1855 most public clocks in Britain showed a single standard time, though the change was not universally welcomed: some towns kept two minute hands on their clock faces, one for railway time and one for their own. The legal recognition of standard time came later, and almost accidentally. In 1858 a court in Dorchester dismissed a case because the defendant had arrived at the courthouse at the correct local time but after the hour set by railway time. The resulting confusion prompted Parliament to act, though it took until 1880 for a statute to define what time it legally was.

Before the 1950s, loading a cargo ship was slow, dangerous work. Goods arrived at the docks in barrels, sacks and crates of every size, and teams of labourers moved each item by hand. A vessel might spend longer in port than at sea, and theft was so routine that it was simply priced into the cost of shipping. The change came from a trucking company owner rather than from the shipping industry itself. His insight was not the metal box, which already existed, but the idea that the box should never be opened between origin and destination. Cranes could lift a sealed container from a lorry directly onto a ship, and the contents would not be handled again until they arrived. Ports resisted. The new system needed different cranes, deeper berths and far fewer dockworkers, and the unions understood immediately what that meant. Several major harbours delayed adoption for a decade and lost their traffic permanently to rivals that had not. The economic effect is hard to overstate. Shipping costs fell so far that where a factory stood mattered much less than it once had, and manufacturing began to move across oceans in ways that would have made no sense before.

Antibiotics work by exploiting differences between bacterial cells and our own. A drug that blocks the construction of a bacterial cell wall, for instance, harms the bacterium and leaves human tissue untouched, because our cells build no such wall. The difficulty is that bacteria reproduce with extraordinary speed. A population can double in twenty minutes, and each division carries a small chance of a copying error. Most errors are harmless or fatal to the cell, but occasionally one produces a bacterium that survives a drug which kills the rest. That survivor then has an entire environment to itself. This is ordinary evolution, running fast enough to watch. What makes it a medical problem rather than a curiosity is the scale on which antibiotics are used. Every course prescribed, and every dose given to farm animals to speed their growth, applies the same pressure to whichever bacteria are present. Developing new antibiotics has proved unexpectedly difficult, and the commercial incentive is weak: a drug taken for a week earns far less than one taken for life. Several large companies have closed their antibiotic programmes entirely, leaving much of the remaining work to universities and small firms.

When a local newspaper closes, the effects reach further than the loss of its reporting. Studies of American towns that lost their paper found that municipal borrowing costs rose afterwards, because lenders had less independent information about how a town was run and priced that uncertainty into their loans. Turnout in local elections fell as well, and the number of candidates standing for office declined. Where nobody reports on a council, fewer people know what it does, and fewer still see a reason to contest a seat on it. National outlets have not filled the gap. Their economics depend on reaching very large audiences, which makes a planning dispute in a town of thirty thousand impossible to justify covering. Online alternatives have appeared in some places, but they tend to concentrate where advertising money already is, which is rarely where the closures happen. Some researchers argue the losses are best understood as a public problem rather than a commercial one, since the benefits of local reporting fall largely on people who never bought the paper. That framing points towards subsidy or foundation funding, neither of which sits comfortably with a press expected to hold power to account.

For most of the twentieth century, sleep was treated as a period in which the brain simply rested. That view has been abandoned. Recordings taken during sleep show patterns of activity as complex as those in waking, and much of it appears to be concerned with the previous day. The clearest evidence comes from experiments in which volunteers learn a task and are then either allowed to sleep or kept awake. Those who sleep perform better the following day, and the improvement is larger than the difference in tiredness can explain. In some studies the sleeping group improves on a skill they did not practise again at all. Exactly what happens is still contested. One account holds that the brain replays the day's sequences at speed, strengthening the connections involved. Another emphasises the opposite process: weakening connections that were not useful, so that the important ones stand out by comparison. The two accounts are not incompatible, and evidence exists for both. What has changed is the underlying assumption. Sleep is no longer regarded as time subtracted from learning, but as a stage of it.

Before 1840, sending a letter in Britain was expensive and paid for by the person who received it. Charges depended on distance and on the number of sheets, which meant that every letter had to be measured and assessed by hand. Recipients who could not pay, or did not wish to, simply refused delivery, and the Post Office absorbed the cost of carrying the letter both ways. The reform proposed a single low charge for any letter under a certain weight, anywhere in the country, paid in advance by the sender. Its author argued that most of the cost lay in handling rather than in transport, so distance should not affect the price at all. Officials objected that revenue would collapse. It did fall at first, and did not recover for years. But the volume of letters rose so sharply that the reform was never seriously reversed, and other countries copied it within a decade. The adhesive stamp itself was almost an afterthought, a practical way to show that postage had been paid. It became the most visible part of a change that was really about pricing.

questions.prompt: The passage is mainly concerned with
options: techniques for measuring temperature differences between cities and countryside
the medical consequences of the 2003 European heat wave
why cities retain heat and why the common responses to it achieve less than they appear to
the history of zoning law in European cities
questions.explanation: The passage first explains the structural causes of urban heat, then argues that visible municipal measures are modest in effect. The heat wave and zoning are mentioned in service of that argument rather than as the subject, and no measurement technique is described anywhere.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, vegetation cools the surrounding air by
questions.explanation: The passage states directly that vegetation cools the air through evaporation. Reflection is what a white roof does, and neither wind nor carbon absorption is mentioned in connection with cooling.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that the 2003 heat wave findings were significant because they
options: demonstrated that white roofs reduce mortality
led Parliament to change how cities are zoned
were the first measurements of urban temperatures ever taken
showed the temperature gap had consequences that could not be explained by who happened to live where
questions.explanation: The detail that the difference persisted after accounting for age and income is what rules out the alternative explanation that city populations simply differ from rural ones. The passage never claims the study was a first, never links roofs to mortality, and describes zoning reform as something researchers argue for rather than something achieved.

questions.prompt: As used in the last sentence, "contentious" most nearly means
questions.explanation: The word describes rethinking how cities are zoned and built, set against the ease of planting trees — the contrast is about political friction, not cost or difficulty. The sentence already supplies "slower" for the practical objection, so the second word must carry something else.

questions.prompt: The author mentions painting roofs white primarily in order to
options: recommend it as the most effective municipal response available
explain the physical process by which solar radiation is reflected
contrast its success with the failure of tree planting
give an example of a measure whose benefits are narrower than they first appear
questions.explanation: The white roof appears in a paragraph arguing that visible measures are local and modest, and the following sentence limits its benefit to the building beneath it. The author groups it with tree planting rather than against it, and never explains the physics of reflection.

questions.prompt: The passage is primarily concerned with
options: the reasons Bristol and London developed at different rates
how a commercial necessity produced a national standard that the law only later confirmed
a legal dispute over the scheduling of court appearances
the engineering difficulties of building railway lines across Britain
questions.explanation: The passage traces standard time from a railway convenience to an 1880 statute, with the law arriving last. The Dorchester case is one step in that sequence rather than the subject, and neither engineering nor regional development is discussed.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, by 1855
options: most public clocks in Britain displayed a single standard time
every town in Britain had adopted two minute hands
railway companies had abandoned local time entirely
Parliament had defined standard time by statute
questions.explanation: The passage gives 1855 as the point when most public clocks showed one standard time. The statute came in 1880, and the two minute hands were something only some towns did.

questions.prompt: The detail about clock faces with two minute hands suggests that some towns
options: were required by Parliament to display both times
found railway time to be frequently inaccurate
profited from selling modified clocks to travellers
accepted the practical need for railway time without giving up their own
questions.explanation: Keeping both hands shows a town using railway time while preserving local time, which is what the passage means by the change not being universally welcomed. Parliament had not yet acted at that point, and nothing suggests railway time was unreliable or commercially exploited.

questions.prompt: As used in the third sentence, "discrepancy" most nearly means
questions.explanation: The word refers back to the ten-minute gap between noon in Bristol and noon in London, which is a difference rather than a delay — neither town was late. No complaint or act of measuring is described.

questions.prompt: The author describes the 1858 Dorchester case primarily to
options: illustrate how unreliable railway schedules had become
explain the specific wording Parliament adopted in 1880
criticize the court for dismissing the case
show that legal recognition trailed a change that had already taken hold in practice
questions.explanation: The case is introduced immediately after the claim that legal recognition came later and almost accidentally, and it demonstrates law catching up to established practice. The author passes no judgement on the court and never quotes the statute.

questions.prompt: The passage is mainly concerned with
options: the engineering problems involved in designing a metal shipping container
the working conditions of dockworkers in the early twentieth century
a dispute between trucking companies and shipping lines over freight rates
how a change in handling cargo reshaped where goods could profitably be made
questions.explanation: The passage moves from the old loading system to the container to its effect on where factories could sit, ending on manufacturing moving across oceans. Dockworkers and the box itself appear in service of that argument rather than as the subject, and no freight-rate dispute is described.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, theft at the docks was
options: rare because goods were counted by hand
the main reason ports resisted the new system
common enough to be treated as a normal cost of shipping
questions.explanation: The passage says theft was so routine it was priced into the cost of shipping. It never claims containers ended it, and the resistance is attributed to cranes, berths and jobs rather than to theft.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that the ports which delayed adoption
options: recovered their traffic once they eventually invested
misjudged how quickly shippers would move to harbours that had converted
were prevented by law from installing the new cranes
lacked the deep water needed for the new vessels
questions.explanation: Traffic was lost 'permanently' to rivals that had adopted, which only makes sense if the delaying ports underestimated how fast shippers would leave. The passage gives no legal obstacle, and 'permanently' rules out recovery.

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, "insight" most nearly means
options: a realisation that others had missed
questions.explanation: The word introduces an idea explicitly contrasted with the metal box that already existed, so it names something understood rather than something built or bought. None of the other options can be 'not the box, but the idea'.

questions.prompt: The author mentions that the metal box already existed in order to
options: suggest that the trucking company owner made no real contribution
locate the real innovation in how the box was used rather than in the object
explain why the containers were made of metal rather than wood
credit the shipping industry with the original invention
questions.explanation: The clause exists to set up the contrast in the same sentence: not the box, but the rule that it stays sealed. The passage credits the outsider rather than the industry, and never discusses materials.

questions.prompt: The passage is primarily about
options: the case for banning all antibiotic use in farming
the chemical structure of the first antibiotics
how bacterial cells differ from human cells
why resistance develops so readily and why replacing the drugs has proved hard
questions.explanation: The passage explains the mechanism of resistance, then turns to the weak incentive to develop replacements. The cell-wall difference and farm use are steps in that argument, and no ban is advocated anywhere.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, a bacterial population can double in
questions.explanation: The figure is stated directly. The week appears elsewhere, describing how long a course of antibiotics is taken, which is a different measurement entirely.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that a resistant bacterium multiplies quickly because
options: it reproduces faster than non-resistant bacteria do
it can pass its resistance to human cells
farm animals carry it between different locations
the drug has removed the competitors it would otherwise have had
questions.explanation: 'That survivor then has an entire environment to itself' means the drug cleared the competition rather than that the survivor is inherently faster. Nothing suggests resistance transfers to human cells.

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, "pressure" most nearly means
options: a force determining which organisms survive
questions.explanation: The word describes what every prescription applies to whatever bacteria are present, in a paragraph about evolution — it names selection, not weight or urgency. The passage never mentions what doctors or patients feel.

questions.prompt: The author contrasts a drug taken for a week with one taken for life in order to
options: criticise the price charged for long-term medication
explain why companies have little reason to develop antibiotics
argue that courses of antibiotics should last longer
show that antibiotics work faster than other medicines
questions.explanation: The contrast appears immediately after 'the commercial incentive is weak' and explains it: a short course earns less. The passage recommends nothing about course length and makes no complaint about pricing.

questions.prompt: The passage is mainly concerned with
options: the wider civic costs of local newspaper closures and why nothing has replaced them
how lenders decide the price of municipal bonds
a decline in the quality of national newspapers
the history of advertising revenue in the print industry
questions.explanation: The passage catalogues effects beyond lost reporting, then explains why neither national nor online outlets fill the gap. Bond pricing is one piece of evidence rather than the subject, and national quality is never discussed.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, borrowing costs rose in affected towns because lenders
options: were charged more by national news outlets
had less independent information about how the town was governed
knew the towns had lost advertising revenue
saw that fewer candidates were standing for office
questions.explanation: The passage states the reason directly: less independent information, priced in as uncertainty. The fall in candidates is listed as a separate effect, not as the cause of the borrowing costs.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that online local outlets have not solved the problem because
options: they are barred from attending council meetings
readers are unwilling to trust reporting published online
their journalists have less experience than those in print
they appear in the places least likely to have lost a newspaper
questions.explanation: They concentrate where advertising money already is, 'which is rarely where the closures happen' — so they emerge in the wrong places. The passage raises no question of trust, access or experience.

questions.prompt: As used in the last paragraph, "framing" most nearly means
options: a way of understanding the issue
questions.explanation: The word refers back to treating the losses as a public rather than commercial problem, and what follows from that view. The other meanings of the word are literal or legal and make no sense of 'points towards subsidy'.

questions.prompt: The author ends by noting that subsidy sits uncomfortably with the press in order to
options: acknowledge a difficulty in the solution just proposed
argue that local newspapers are not worth saving
praise foundations for the funding they already provide
explain why national outlets refuse to accept public money
questions.explanation: The sentence immediately follows the proposal of subsidy or foundation funding and qualifies it: a press funded this way is meant to hold power to account. It concedes a problem rather than rejecting the whole idea.

questions.prompt: The passage is primarily concerned with
options: a disagreement about how many hours of sleep adults require
the medical consequences of long-term sleep deprivation
how sleep came to be understood as part of learning rather than a pause in it
techniques for recording brain activity during sleep
questions.explanation: The passage opens with the old view, presents the evidence that displaced it, and closes on sleep as a stage of learning. Recording techniques are mentioned once as evidence, and neither deprivation nor sleep duration is discussed.

questions.prompt: In the experiments described, volunteers who were allowed to sleep
options: reported feeling less tired but performed the same
needed to practise the task a second time
performed better the following day than those kept awake
learned the task more quickly at the outset
questions.explanation: The passage states that sleepers perform better the next day. It explicitly says the gain is larger than tiredness explains, and that in some studies no further practice occurred.

questions.prompt: The detail that some volunteers improved without practising again suggests that
options: the waking group had been practising incorrectly
tiredness had no effect at all on performance
the gain came from sleep itself rather than from additional rehearsal
the task was too easy to require any practice
questions.explanation: Removing further practice removes the obvious alternative explanation, leaving sleep as the source of the improvement. The passage says tiredness explains part of the difference, just not all of it.

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, "contested" most nearly means
questions.explanation: The word introduces two competing accounts of the same process, so it marks disagreement rather than difficulty or novelty. The passage then presents both sides, which is what a contested question looks like.

questions.prompt: The author notes that the two accounts are not incompatible in order to
options: show that the second account has replaced the first
argue that neither explanation has evidence behind it
suggest that the question has now been settled
stop the disagreement being read as one theory defeating the other
questions.explanation: The sentence follows two opposed-sounding explanations and says evidence exists for both, heading off the assumption that one must win. The next sentences make clear the settled part is the assumption about sleep, not the mechanism.

questions.prompt: The passage is mainly about
options: the financial troubles of the British Post Office in the 1840s
the invention and design of the first adhesive stamps
how other countries built their own postal services
a change in how postage was priced, of which the stamp was only the visible sign
questions.explanation: The passage describes the old pricing, the proposed replacement, the objection and the outcome, closing by saying the change was really about pricing. The stamp gets one sentence, and other countries a clause.

questions.prompt: Before the reform, the cost of sending a letter depended on
options: the distance travelled and the number of sheets
the value of whatever was described inside
whether the sender had paid in advance
questions.explanation: Both factors are stated directly. Weight belongs to the reform rather than the old system, and advance payment by the sender is precisely what the reform introduced.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that refused deliveries were costly because
options: recipients were fined for turning letters away
the letter had already been carried and nothing was collected for it
senders demanded compensation for the delay
refused letters had to be stored indefinitely
questions.explanation: The Post Office 'absorbed the cost of carrying the letter both ways', which only makes sense if the work was already done and unpaid. No fines, storage or compensation appear anywhere.

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, "afterthought" most nearly means
options: something added late and of secondary importance
an idea borrowed from another country
questions.explanation: The word is set against the pricing reform as the thing that actually mattered, and the next sentence calls the stamp merely the most visible part. It marks the stamp as minor, not as hasty or foreign.

questions.prompt: The author mentions that revenue did fall at first primarily to
options: concede that the officials' objection was partly justified
show that other countries were right to wait
criticise the reform's author for poor forecasting
explain why the reform was eventually reversed
questions.explanation: The admission sits directly after the officials' objection and directly before 'But the volume of letters rose' — a concession before the counter-argument. The passage says the reform was never reversed and that other countries copied it quickly.

questions.prompt: Because the factory upgraded its filters last year, emissions in the surrounding valley have fallen sharply since then.
options: Residents of the area pressured the plant into cutting the pollution it had produced for years.
The plant is scheduled to upgrade its filtering equipment next year, which should reduce local pollution.
The factory installed new filters because pollution in the surrounding area had already begun to drop.
The air in that area has become considerably cleaner as a result of equipment the plant installed twelve months ago.
questions.explanation: The source says the upgrade came first and caused the drop. The first wrong option reverses that order, making the drop the reason for the upgrade. The second moves the upgrade into the future when it has already happened. The third makes residents the cause, which the source never mentions.

questions.prompt: Unless the museum secures additional funding, it will be forced to close its two smallest galleries by December.
options: Donors have decided to withdraw support for the museum's two smallest galleries before December.
The museum closed its two smallest galleries in December after failing to raise enough money.
Shutting the pair of minor exhibition rooms before the end of the year can only be avoided if more money is found.
The museum will close its two smallest galleries by December, even if it secures additional funding.
questions.explanation: The source makes the closure conditional on funding not arriving. The first wrong option removes the condition, making closure happen regardless. The second reports the closure as already complete. The third turns the museum into the object of a donor decision, when the source only describes what the museum itself will be forced to do.

questions.prompt: The council approved the housing plan only after developers agreed to fund a new access road.
options: The council is expected to approve the housing plan once developers begin building the access road.
Approval for the residential scheme depended on the builders committing to pay for additional infrastructure.
The council agreed to pay for a new access road so that developers would approve the housing plan.
Developers agreed to fund a new access road only after the council had approved the housing plan.
questions.explanation: In the source the developers' commitment came first and made approval possible. The first wrong option puts approval first, reversing what depended on what. The second swaps who pays and who approves. The third presents the approval as still pending when the source says it has happened.

questions.prompt: Although sales rose sharply in the final quarter, the company still ended the year with a loss.
options: Sales are expected to rise sharply next quarter, which should move the company out of loss.
A strong closing three months were not enough to prevent the firm finishing twelve months in deficit.
Because sales rose sharply in the final quarter, the company managed to end the year profitably.
The company's competitors saw sales rise sharply in the final quarter while it recorded a loss.
questions.explanation: The source concedes a good quarter but reports a bad year. The first wrong option turns the concession into a cause and the loss into a profit. The second moves the rise into the future. The third attributes the rise to competitors rather than to the company itself.

questions.prompt: Residents were warned that the bridge would remain closed until engineers completed a full structural survey.
options: Engineers will carry out a structural survey only after the bridge has been reopened to traffic.
The bridge reopened as soon as engineers had begun their structural survey.
Residents demanded that engineers close the bridge until a full structural survey was carried out.
The crossing will not reopen before specialists have finished checking whether it is sound.
questions.explanation: The source makes reopening wait for a completed survey. The first wrong option has the bridge open when the survey merely started. The second puts the survey after reopening, reversing the dependency. The third makes residents the ones demanding closure, when they were only warned of it.

questions.prompt: The policy succeeded in rural districts but had almost no measurable effect in the larger cities.
options: The policy worked well in the largest cities but achieved little in rural districts.
The policy is expected to succeed in rural districts before it reaches the larger cities.
Rural districts adopted the policy while the larger cities rejected it outright.
What worked in the countryside made hardly any difference in major urban centres.
questions.explanation: The source pairs rural success with urban ineffectiveness. The first wrong option swaps which side each outcome belongs to. The second replaces a difference in effect with a difference in whether the policy was adopted at all. The third turns a reported result into a forecast.

questions.prompt: Unless attendance improves substantially over the summer, the festival organisers say that next year's event may be cancelled.
options: The organisers cancelled this year's festival after attendance failed to improve over the summer.
Scrapping the following year's gathering can be avoided only by a marked rise in visitor numbers.
The festival will be cancelled next year even if attendance improves substantially over the summer.
Visitors have told the organisers that they will not attend next year's festival unless it improves.
questions.explanation: The source makes cancellation conditional on attendance staying low. The first wrong option removes the condition so cancellation happens regardless. The second reports a cancellation that has already occurred. The third swaps who is issuing the warning, making visitors rather than organisers the ones setting a condition.

questions.prompt: The law was intended to protect tenants, but landlords found several ways to work around it.
options: The law was intended to protect landlords, but tenants found several ways to work around it.
The law will be introduced to protect tenants, though landlords are already preparing ways around it.
Because landlords found ways around the law, it was later rewritten to protect tenants.
Although drafted to shield renters, the legislation left property owners with a number of loopholes.
questions.explanation: The source names tenants as the intended beneficiaries and landlords as the ones evading. The first wrong option swaps those two roles. The second makes the evasion the reason the law exists rather than a response to it. The third presents the law as not yet in force.

questions.prompt: Because the company failed to renew its licence, it was barred from bidding for public contracts last year.
options: The company was barred from public contracts, and as a result its licence was not renewed.
The company will lose the right to bid for public contracts unless it renews its licence.
Public authorities failed to renew the company's licence, which is why it could not bid.
An expired permit is what kept the firm out of government tenders during the previous twelve months.
questions.explanation: The licence lapsed first and the ban followed. The first wrong option reverses that order. The second makes the authorities responsible for the lapse when the company was. The third turns a completed exclusion into a future risk.

questions.prompt: Although the museum doubled its opening hours, visitor numbers rose only slightly over the following year.
options: Twice as much access brought in barely more people across the next twelve months.
The museum plans to double its opening hours in the hope of attracting more visitors.
Visitor numbers rose so slightly that the museum decided to double its opening hours.
Visitors persuaded the museum to double its opening hours after numbers began to fall.
questions.explanation: The extra hours came first and produced almost nothing. The first wrong option makes the weak numbers the reason for extending hours. The second moves the change into the future. The third invents visitors as the cause.

questions.prompt: The regulation applies to every vessel over twenty metres, regardless of where the vessel is registered.
options: From next year the regulation will begin to apply to vessels over twenty metres.
Vessels over twenty metres must register the regulation wherever they operate.
Vessels are registered according to their length, which determines whether the regulation applies.
Ships longer than that measurement fall under the rule no matter which country issued their papers.
questions.explanation: Length decides whether the rule applies; registration is explicitly irrelevant. The first wrong option makes registration depend on length. The second swaps what registers what. The third makes a current rule a future one.

questions.prompt: Sales of the device collapsed once a cheaper rival appeared, despite years of favourable reviews.
options: Favourable reviews caused a cheaper rival to enter the market and take the device's sales.
A less expensive competitor destroyed demand for the product, even though critics had praised it for a long time.
Reviewers turned against the device once a cheaper rival appeared, and sales collapsed.
Sales of the device are expected to fall if a cheaper rival reaches the market.
questions.explanation: The rival caused the collapse; the good reviews are a concession that failed to prevent it. The first wrong option makes the reviews the cause. The second turns a completed collapse into a forecast. The third makes reviewers change their view, which the source denies.

questions.prompt: Unless the council receives objections within thirty days, the planning application will be approved automatically.
options: The council approved the planning application after thirty days of objections were considered.
Silence from the public for a month means the building request goes through without further review.
The council must object within thirty days or the applicant may proceed with building.
The planning application will be rejected automatically if no objections arrive within thirty days.
questions.explanation: No objections means approval. The first wrong option inverts the outcome to rejection. The second reports the approval as already given after objections. The third makes the council the objector rather than the public.

questions.prompt: The drug performed well in laboratory tests but showed no benefit when trialled on human patients.
options: Patients reported no benefit, which led researchers to repeat the laboratory tests.
The drug helped human patients even though laboratory tests had suggested it would not.
Promising results under controlled conditions did not carry over to people.
The drug has performed well in the laboratory and will shortly be tested on patients.
questions.explanation: It worked in the lab and failed in people. The first wrong option reverses both halves. The second puts the human trial in the future when it has happened. The third makes patient reports cause new lab work, which the source does not say.

questions.prompt: Rather than closing the branch entirely, the bank reduced its hours and kept two staff on site.
options: Two members of staff kept the branch open after the bank decided to close it.
The office stayed open with a smaller team and shorter times instead of shutting altogether.
The bank closed the branch entirely rather than reduce its hours.
The bank intends to reduce the branch's hours before deciding whether to close it.
questions.explanation: The branch stayed open in reduced form. The first wrong option chooses the opposite of the two alternatives. The second makes staff act against a closure decision. The third turns a settled outcome into an undecided plan.

questions.prompt: Because the report was published during the holidays, almost no journalists noticed its most serious findings.
options: Journalists ignored the report, so it was published during the holidays.
Timing the release for a quiet period meant the gravest conclusions went largely unreported.
The report will be published during the holidays, when few journalists are working.
Journalists published the report during the holidays and overlooked its most serious findings.
questions.explanation: Publishing during the holidays is why the findings were missed. The first wrong option makes being ignored the reason for the timing. The second moves publication into the future. The third makes journalists the publishers.

questions.prompt: The new rule bans advertising aimed at children, though existing campaigns may continue until December.
options: Existing campaigns must stop immediately, while new advertising aimed at children remains permitted.
Advertisers have banned campaigns aimed at children, and the rule allows them until December.
From December the new rule will begin to ban advertising aimed at children.
Marketing directed at young people is now forbidden, but adverts already running have until the end of the year.
questions.explanation: New adverts are banned now; existing ones get until December. The first wrong option swaps which category is protected. The second makes December the start of the ban rather than the end of the exemption. The third makes advertisers the ones imposing the ban.

questions.prompt: Farmers who switched to the new seed reported higher yields, but only in fields with good drainage.
options: Seed producers, rather than farmers, reported the higher yields from the new variety.
The variety produced bigger harvests for growers, though the gain appeared solely where water drained well.
Farmers expect higher yields once they switch to the new seed next season.
Good drainage was the result of switching to the new seed, which raised yields.
questions.explanation: Drainage is the condition under which the seed helps, not something the seed caused. The first wrong option makes drainage an effect. The second changes who reported the result. The third turns a measured outcome into an expectation.

questions.prompt: The city introduced free transport on weekends, and car use in the centre fell sharply within months.
options: Removing fares at the end of the week quickly cut how much people drove downtown.
The city hopes that free weekend transport will eventually reduce car use in the centre.
Drivers made transport free at weekends in order to reduce congestion in the centre.
Car use in the centre fell, which persuaded the city to make weekend transport free.
questions.explanation: Free transport came first and driving fell after. The first wrong option reverses cause and effect. The second turns a measured fall into a hope. The third makes drivers set the fares.

questions.prompt: Although both machines cost the same to buy, the older model is far more expensive to run.
options: Buyers of the older machine pay more for it, though both cost the same to operate.
The older machine is cheaper to run, although it costs more to buy than the newer one.
The older model will become more expensive to run once the new pricing takes effect.
The two devices carry an identical purchase price, but keeping the earlier one working costs much more.
questions.explanation: Same purchase price, different running cost. The first wrong option swaps which cost differs. The second makes a present fact conditional on future pricing. The third moves the difference back to the purchase price.

questions.prompt: Nurses were given the training first, and doctors received the same course several months later.
options: Doctors will receive the training several months after the nurses have finished it.
Because doctors had already taken the course, nurses were trained several months later.
Doctors were trained first, and nurses took the same course months afterwards.
The nursing staff completed the programme well before their medical colleagues were offered it.
questions.explanation: Nurses went first. The first wrong option makes the doctors' training the reason for the delay. The second swaps which group went first. The third leaves the doctors' training still to come, when the source reports it as done.

questions.prompt: The bridge was designed to last a century but required major repairs after only thirty years.
options: Intended to survive a hundred years, the crossing needed serious work in less than a third of that time.
The bridge is expected to need major repairs about thirty years from now.
The bridge needed repairs after thirty years, so it was redesigned to last a century.
Engineers who repaired the bridge had designed it to last a hundred years.
questions.explanation: The design intention failed well short. The first wrong option makes the repairs the reason for the design. The second puts the repairs in the future. The third claims the repairers were the designers, which the source never says.

questions.prompt: Because it rained throughout the festival, organisers offered refunds to anyone who left before the final day.
options: Organisers offered refunds, and as a result many people left before the festival's final day.
Organisers will offer refunds if it rains throughout the festival next year.
Festival-goers demanded refunds from the organisers once the rain began.
Constant wet weather led the people running the event to pay back those who departed early.
questions.explanation: Rain caused the refunds. The first wrong option makes the refunds cause the early departures. The second turns a past response into a future condition. The third makes attendees demand what organisers in fact offered.

questions.prompt: The law passed easily in the lower house but stalled for eighteen months in the senate.
options: The law is expected to pass the lower house before spending months in the senate.
Senators introduced the law in the lower house, where it stalled for eighteen months.
The senate passed the law quickly, but the lower house delayed it for eighteen months.
One chamber approved the bill without difficulty while the other held it up for a year and a half.
questions.explanation: Easy passage in one chamber, long delay in the other. The first wrong option swaps which chamber did which. The second makes both stages future. The third moves the delay to the wrong chamber and adds an introduction the source never mentions.

questions.prompt: Although she had never studied economics formally, her analysis proved more accurate than the bank's own forecasts.
options: The bank's economists produced a more accurate forecast than she did, despite her lack of training.
She is studying economics now and expects her forecasts to improve on the bank's.
Her formal training in economics is what made her analysis better than the bank's.
Without any training in the subject she still predicted events better than the institution's professional projections did.
questions.explanation: She had no formal training and still did better. The first wrong option credits training she never had. The second swaps who was more accurate. The third makes her accuracy a future hope rather than a demonstrated result.

questions.prompt: The scheme was suspended after auditors found that a quarter of the payments could not be explained.
options: The scheme was suspended, which is why auditors were unable to explain a quarter of the payments.
Inspectors identified twenty-five per cent of the transfers as unaccounted for, and the programme was halted.
Those running the scheme suspended the auditors after a quarter of payments were questioned.
Auditors will suspend the scheme if they cannot explain a quarter of the payments.
questions.explanation: The audit finding caused the suspension. The first wrong option makes the suspension the reason the payments could not be explained. The second turns it into a condition. The third swaps who suspended whom, which reverses the whole situation.

questions.prompt: Even though the software was free, most schools chose the paid alternative because it came with support.
options: Institutions mostly bought the commercial product for its assistance, despite a version costing nothing being available.
Schools will switch to the paid alternative once support for the free version ends.
Schools chose the free software because the paid alternative offered no support.
Software companies gave schools the paid version free of charge, along with support.
questions.explanation: Support is why schools paid rather than took the free option. The first wrong option flips which product had support and which was chosen. The second removes the payment entirely. The third turns a completed choice into a future switch.

questions.prompt: Production stopped for six weeks while the factory replaced equipment that had been in use since 1998.
options: The factory will stop production for six weeks in order to replace ageing equipment.
The factory replaced its equipment because production had already stopped for six weeks.
Equipment suppliers halted production at the factory for six weeks while carrying out replacements.
The plant halted output for a month and a half to install machinery replacing what had run for decades.
questions.explanation: The replacement is why production stopped. The first wrong option makes the stoppage the reason for replacing. The second puts a completed shutdown in the future. The third makes suppliers rather than the factory halt production.

questions.prompt: The charity spends less on administration than almost any comparable organisation, according to its published accounts.
options: Its own financial statements show that running costs are lower there than at nearly all similar bodies.
The charity's published accounts show it spends more on administration than similar organisations.
An outside auditor, rather than the charity itself, published the comparison of administrative costs.
The charity intends to reduce its administrative spending below that of comparable organisations.
questions.explanation: It already spends less, on its own published figures. The first wrong option reverses the comparison. The second changes who published the accounts. The third makes an existing position into an intention.

questions.prompt: Tickets sold out within an hour, although the venue had added two extra performances that morning.
options: The venue will add two extra performances if tickets sell out within an hour.
Even with a pair of additional shows announced earlier that day, everything was gone in sixty minutes.
The venue added two extra performances because tickets had not sold quickly enough.
Ticket agents added two extra performances after the venue sold out within an hour.
questions.explanation: Extra shows were added and everything still sold instantly. The first wrong option makes slow sales the reason for adding them. The second makes the additions conditional and future. The third puts the additions after the sell-out and credits agents.

questions.prompt: The virus spreads easily but causes serious illness in only a small proportion of those infected.
options: The virus is expected to spread easily once restrictions are lifted next month.
Those infected spread serious illness to a small proportion of the people they meet.
The virus rarely spreads, but almost everyone who catches it becomes seriously ill.
Transmission happens readily, though few of the people who catch it become badly unwell.
questions.explanation: It spreads widely but rarely does serious harm. The first wrong option inverts both halves. The second turns a current property into a forecast. The third makes the small proportion describe who gets infected rather than who becomes seriously ill.

questions.prompt: The committee rejected the proposal twice before finally accepting a version that had barely changed at all.
options: The person who wrote the proposal rejected the committee's changes twice before agreeing.
After two refusals the panel approved something almost identical to what it had turned down.
The committee accepted the proposal at once and rejected the later revised versions.
The committee is expected to reject the proposal twice before accepting a revised version.
questions.explanation: Two rejections came first, then acceptance of nearly the same thing. The first wrong option reverses the order of acceptance and rejection. The second makes it a prediction. The third swaps who rejected whom.

questions.prompt: The library extended its opening hours last winter, but the number of borrowed books stayed almost exactly the same.
options: Readers themselves extended the library's opening hours, though the number of books borrowed hardly changed.
The library will extend its opening hours next winter in the hope that more books are borrowed.
Because borrowing stayed at the same level, the library decided to extend its opening hours last winter.
Keeping the doors unlocked for longer over the cold months produced no real change in how much people read.
questions.explanation: The longer hours came first and changed nothing. The first wrong option makes the unchanged borrowing the reason for the longer hours. The second gives readers a power only the library has. The third moves a finished experiment into the future.

questions.prompt: Although the new bus route reaches the hospital in half the time, very few passengers have chosen to use it.
options: Hardly anyone travels on the service despite it cutting the journey to the medical centre by fifty per cent.
Hospital staff selected the new bus route, although very few other passengers travel on it.
Because so many passengers now use the new route, the journey to the hospital takes half the time.
The new bus route will halve the journey time once enough passengers agree to use it.
questions.explanation: The route is much faster and still almost empty. The first wrong option makes heavy use the reason for the speed. The second invents hospital staff as the ones who chose it. The third makes the time saving depend on future demand.

questions.prompt: The teacher marked the essays before the holiday, and returned them to the students on the first day back.
options: The teacher gave the essays back before the holiday and marked them once the students returned.
Students marked one another's essays over the holiday and gave them to the teacher afterwards.
Grading was finished ahead of the break, with each piece of work handed over as soon as classes resumed.
The teacher will mark the essays during the holiday and hand them back when term begins.
questions.explanation: Marking happened before the holiday and handing back after it. The first wrong option reverses those two events. The second makes the students the markers. The third leaves the marking still to be done.

questions.prompt: Prices in the market fall every autumn, because farmers harvest more fruit than the town can possibly eat.
options: Prices are expected to fall next autumn if farmers gather more fruit than usual.
Each year the crop is bigger than local appetite, so what shoppers pay drops when the season arrives.
Farmers grow extra fruit in autumn because prices in the market have already come down.
Traders in the town cut their prices every autumn so that farmers will gather more fruit.
questions.explanation: A surplus of fruit is what pushes prices down. The first wrong option makes the low prices the reason for growing more. The second makes traders act in order to influence farmers. The third turns a yearly pattern into a single forecast.

questions.prompt: The village had no doctor for eleven years, until a clinic opened in the old school building last spring.
options: The village doctor opened a clinic in the old school building after eleven years of waiting.
The village still has no doctor, but a clinic is due to open in the old school.
A clinic opened in the old school eleven years before the village lost its last doctor.
Medical care returned to the settlement only when premises were converted for that purpose, after more than a decade.
questions.explanation: Eleven years without a doctor ended when the clinic opened. The first wrong option puts the clinic before the gap instead of after it. The second invents a village doctor who was in fact absent. The third leaves the clinic unopened.

questions.prompt: Most of the students who failed the first test passed easily when they took it again in June.
options: Nearly everyone unsuccessful at the initial attempt found the repeat straightforward a few months later.
Most students who succeeded at the first test were unable to pass when they sat it a second time.
Students who failed the first test will be allowed to take it again in June.
The examiners passed most of the failing students without asking them to sit the paper again.
questions.explanation: Those who failed first time went on to succeed second time. The first wrong option swaps which attempt was the successful one. The second removes the resit and makes the examiners award the pass. The third turns a completed resit into a future permission.

questions.prompt: The factory produces twice as much as it did five years ago, but employs fewer than half the workers.
options: The factory now employs twice as many staff but makes less than half of what it once did.
Output has doubled over that period while the number of people on the payroll has more than halved.
The factory expects to double its output and halve its workforce within the next five years.
Workers at the factory have halved their own numbers in order to double what the machines make.
questions.explanation: Production doubled and staffing more than halved. The first wrong option swaps which figure rose and which fell. The second makes the workers themselves responsible for cutting the workforce. The third turns a measured change into a plan.

questions.prompt: She refused the promotion twice before accepting a similar role at a smaller company the following year.
options: After turning down the senior post on two occasions, she took an equivalent job elsewhere twelve months later.
The smaller company rejected her twice before offering the senior position she had wanted.
She accepted the promotion immediately and turned down a comparable position at a smaller company afterwards.
She has refused the promotion twice and may accept a comparable position elsewhere next year.
questions.explanation: Two refusals came first, then an equivalent job somewhere else. The first wrong option reverses which offer she accepted. The second makes the company the one doing the rejecting. The third leaves the second job undecided.

questions.prompt: The council approved the development only after the builder agreed to fund a new road to the site.
options: The council will approve the development if the builder promises to fund a new road.
Permission was granted purely on condition that the construction firm paid for improved access itself.
The council undertook to build the new road itself once the developer's application had been approved.
The builder agreed to fund the new road only after the council had already approved the development.
questions.explanation: The builder's promise came first and the approval followed. The first wrong option reverses that order. The second makes the council pay for the road. The third turns a decision already taken into a condition still to be met.

questions.prompt: Because the samples were stored at the wrong temperature, the laboratory had to repeat the entire experiment.
options: The scientists blamed the delivery company for repeating the experiment with badly stored samples.
Incorrect refrigeration of the material forced staff to run the whole study a second time.
The samples were kept at the wrong temperature because the experiment had to be carried out twice.
If the samples are kept at the wrong temperature, the laboratory will have to repeat the experiment.
questions.explanation: Bad storage is why the work had to be done again. The first wrong option makes the repetition the reason for the bad storage. The second hands the repeat to an outside company. The third turns a completed setback into a warning.

questions.prompt: The treaty allows each country to inspect the other's facilities twice a year, without giving advance notice.
options: An international body examines the facilities of both countries twice a year without warning them first.
Each country must give advance notice before entering the other's facilities, which it may do twice yearly.
Under the agreement either state may examine its counterpart's installations on two occasions annually with no warning beforehand.
From next year the treaty will let each country enter the other's facilities twice annually.
questions.explanation: Each side may inspect the other twice yearly with no warning. The first wrong option adds the notice the treaty removes. The second replaces the two countries with an outside inspector. The third makes a rule already in force begin later.

questions.prompt: Sales rose sharply in the months after the advertisement was withdrawn, which surprised almost everyone at the agency.
options: Removing the commercial was followed by a steep climb in revenue that few people working there had predicted.
Advertisers withdrew from the agency, whose own sales rose sharply in the months afterwards.
The advertisement was pulled because sales had already risen sharply, to the surprise of the agency.
Sales are expected to rise sharply once the advertisement is withdrawn later this year.
questions.explanation: The advertisement went first and the rise came afterwards. The first wrong option makes the rise the reason for withdrawing it. The second changes what was withdrawn and whose sales rose. The third turns a recorded rise into a forecast.

questions.prompt: Inspectors closed the plant after discovering that waste had been discharged into the river for several months.
options: The plant's owners closed it themselves and reported the discharge to the inspectors.
Inspectors will close the plant if they find that waste has been released into the river.
The site was shut down when officials found a long-running release of pollution into local water.
Waste was released into the river after inspectors had already closed the plant down.
questions.explanation: The discharge came first and the closure followed the discovery. The first wrong option puts the pollution after the closure. The second makes the owners close the plant and report themselves. The third turns a completed shutdown into a threat.

questions.prompt: Although the equipment was donated free of charge, installing it cost the hospital more than buying it would have.
options: The hospital donated the equipment and paid another organisation to install it free of charge.
The equipment will be donated free of charge, though installation is expected to be expensive.
The hospital paid for the equipment because accepting a donation would have cost even more.
Setting up the gift proved dearer for the medical centre than a straightforward purchase.
questions.explanation: The gift was free but fitting it cost more than buying would have. The first wrong option has the hospital buy rather than accept the donation. The second makes the hospital the donor. The third puts an accomplished expense in the future.

questions.prompt: The editor rejected the article twice, but published it without changes once a rival journal expressed interest.
options: A rival journal turned the article down twice, and the editor printed it once interest appeared.
The editor printed the article twice before a rival journal turned it down without explanation.
The editor will print the article unchanged if a rival journal shows any interest in it.
Two refusals were reversed the moment a competing publication showed enthusiasm, and the piece appeared unaltered.
questions.explanation: Two rejections were followed by unchanged publication once a competitor showed interest. The first wrong option swaps which act happened twice. The second moves the rejections to the rival journal. The third makes the publication conditional and future.

questions.prompt: Farmers in the valley abandoned the traditional crop when a cheaper import made it impossible to compete.
options: A cheaper import appeared in the valley because farmers there had already given up the traditional crop.
Importers gave up the traditional crop once farmers in the valley began selling it more cheaply.
Farmers in the valley will give up the traditional crop if a cheaper import reaches the market.
Growers gave up their old variety because goods arriving from abroad undercut them completely.
questions.explanation: The cheap import is what drove the crop out. The first wrong option makes the abandonment the reason for the import. The second swaps the roles of importers and farmers. The third turns a completed change into a possibility.

questions.prompt: The medicine works only when taken with food, which many patients discover after their first ineffective dose.
options: Patients will be told to take the medicine with food once the first trial results are published.
Doctors take the first dose with food in order to find out whether the medicine works.
A meal must accompany the drug for it to have any effect, as people often learn the hard way.
The medicine works only on an empty stomach, which patients realise after eating with their first dose.
questions.explanation: Food is required for the drug to work at all. The first wrong option reverses the condition to an empty stomach. The second makes doctors rather than patients take the dose. The third replaces present practice with a future instruction.

questions.prompt: Rents in the district doubled within three years, forcing many long-established shops to move to cheaper streets.
options: Rents in the district are likely to double, which would force many old shops to move away.
Shops moved away to cheaper streets, and rents in the district doubled as a result.
Shopkeepers doubled the rents over three years, which forced the district's landlords to move away.
A hundred per cent rise in what businesses paid over that short period pushed old traders elsewhere.
questions.explanation: The rent rise is what drove the shops out. The first wrong option makes the departures the cause of the rise. The second has tenants setting rents and landlords leaving. The third turns a recorded doubling into a prediction.

questions.prompt: The bank refused the loan not because the business was unprofitable but because its records were incomplete.
options: The business turned down the bank's offer because the paperwork the lender supplied was incomplete.
The bank will turn the application down unless the business completes its paperwork before the deadline.
Missing paperwork, rather than any lack of earnings, is what led the lender to turn the application down.
The bank turned the application down because the business was losing money, although its paperwork was in order.
questions.explanation: Incomplete records, not poor profits, explain the refusal. The first wrong option swaps the reason given for the reason denied. The second makes the business the party that refuses. The third turns a decision already made into a warning.

questions.prompt: Volunteers cleared the beach every weekend, yet the amount of plastic washed ashore did not noticeably decrease.
options: Plastic stopped arriving on the shore, so volunteers no longer needed to clear the beach at weekends.
Weekly unpaid clean-ups made no visible difference to how much rubbish the sea kept depositing on the sand.
The local council cleared the beach each weekend while volunteers measured the plastic arriving there.
Volunteers will clear the beach every weekend until the plastic arriving there begins to fall.
questions.explanation: Regular clearing failed to reduce the incoming plastic. The first wrong option ends the problem and with it the clearing. The second gives the work to the council and the measuring to the volunteers. The third turns a completed effort into an ongoing plan.

questions.prompt: The species survived the drought in the north but disappeared completely from the drier valleys further south.
options: The species is expected to come through the coming drought in the north but not further south.
Populations endured the dry spell at the upper end of the range while vanishing entirely lower down.
Farmers in the southern valleys removed the species, which continued to live on in the north.
The species died out in the north but came through the drought in the drier southern valleys.
questions.explanation: It held on in the north and was lost in the south. The first wrong option swaps the two regions. The second invents farmers as the cause of the southern loss. The third turns a past drought into one still to come.

questions.prompt: Students who took notes by hand remembered more of the lecture than those who typed on laptops.
options: Writing with a pen produced better recall of the talk than using a keyboard did.
Students working on laptops retained more of the lecture than those writing with a pen.
Students will be asked to write their notes by hand so that they retain more of the lecture.
Lecturers who wrote by hand were remembered better than those who used a laptop in class.
questions.explanation: Handwriting beat typing for memory. The first wrong option reverses which group did better. The second makes the lecturers rather than the students the ones writing. The third turns a finding into an instruction not yet given.

questions.prompt: Had the warning been issued a week earlier, the evacuation could have been completed before the storm arrived.
options: Seven more days of notice would have allowed everyone to leave safely ahead of the bad weather.
The alert came a week early, which is why everyone had left before the storm arrived.
Residents issued their own alert a week before the storm and left the area in time.
If the alert is given a week earlier next time, everyone will be able to leave before the storm.
questions.explanation: The warning was late and the evacuation was therefore unfinished. The first wrong option treats the imagined early warning as something that actually happened. The second makes the residents issue it. The third turns a regret about the past into a plan for a future storm.

questions.prompt: The measure reduced accidents on the busiest roads, though it had no effect at all on quieter routes.
options: The measure is expected to cut crashes on the busiest roads once it comes into force.
Crashes fell where traffic was heaviest, but nothing changed along less crowded stretches.
The measure cut crashes on the emptier stretches while leaving the heaviest traffic entirely unaffected.
Drivers on the busiest roads introduced the measure themselves, and crashes fell as a result.
questions.explanation: It worked where traffic was heavy and nowhere else. The first wrong option swaps which kind of road benefited. The second makes drivers rather than an authority impose it. The third turns a measured result into an expectation.

questions.prompt: What appears to be generosity is often self-interest, since donors gain influence that money could not otherwise buy.
options: Apparent kindness frequently serves the giver, who acquires a standing no payment on its own would secure.
Givers will eventually acquire influence if their apparent kindness continues for long enough.
People give because they already hold influence, not in order to obtain any for themselves.
Those who receive the gifts gain the standing that the giver's money could never have purchased.
questions.explanation: Giving looks selfless but wins the giver influence. The first wrong option reverses cause and effect by making existing influence the motive. The second transfers the benefit to the recipient. The third turns a general truth into a future outcome.

questions.prompt: The author revised the manuscript for nine years, yet reviewers criticised precisely the passages she had rewritten most.
options: The author intends to spend nine years reworking the sections that reviewers have attacked.
Nearly a decade of reworking produced exactly the sections that critics singled out for attack.
Reviewers praised the very sections the author had reworked most during her nine years of revision.
Reviewers spent nine years reworking the manuscript, and the author attacked the sections they changed.
questions.explanation: The most reworked passages drew the harshest criticism. The first wrong option turns the criticism into praise. The second makes the reviewers the revisers and the author the critic. The third makes the long revision a future intention.

questions.prompt: Because so few records survive from that century, historians rely heavily on the accounts of a single traveller.
options: Historians ignore the lone traveller's testimony because so much other material from the period is available.
A single traveller collected the few documents from the period on which scholars now depend.
The scarcity of remaining documents leaves scholars dependent almost entirely on what one visitor wrote down.
Scholars will have to depend on one traveller's testimony once the remaining documents are lost.
questions.explanation: Because almost nothing else survives, one traveller's account carries the weight. The first wrong option reverses the scarcity and the dependence. The second turns the traveller into a collector of other people's documents. The third places the dependence in a future that has not arrived.

questions.prompt: The policy was defended on economic grounds, although its architects had originally proposed it for entirely political reasons.
options: The plan was first put forward to improve the economy and only later justified in political terms.
Money became the public justification for a plan its designers first put forward to serve party purposes.
The plan will be justified in economic terms once its political origins have been forgotten.
Opponents of the plan, rather than the people who wrote it, argued that its aims were political.
questions.explanation: Political motives came first, economic arguments came later. The first wrong option swaps the two around. The second moves the political claim from the authors to their opponents. The third makes an existing defence something still to come.

questions.prompt: Only after the third audit did anyone notice that the same signature appeared on every one of the receipts.
options: It took three separate examinations before it became clear that a single hand had signed all the documents.
A third examination will be needed before anyone can check whether the handwriting on the documents matches.
The people carrying out the examinations had themselves signed all the documents, as nobody realised.
The identical handwriting was spotted immediately, which is why a third examination was eventually ordered.
questions.explanation: The pattern went unnoticed until the third check. The first wrong option claims it was seen at once. The second makes the auditors the forgers. The third leaves the third check still to happen.

questions.prompt: The invention spread quickly across the continent, but it took almost two centuries to reach the islands offshore.
options: Islanders carried the device to the mainland, where it then moved rapidly for two hundred years.
The device is moving rapidly across the mainland and should reach the outlying islands within two hundred years.
What moved rapidly through the mainland needed nearly two hundred years to arrive on the outlying land masses.
The device appeared first on the outlying islands and only moved onto the mainland two hundred years later.
questions.explanation: It travelled fast on land and reached the islands only much later. The first wrong option reverses which place had it first. The second makes islanders the carriers. The third turns a completed spread into one still under way.

questions.prompt: After weeks of negotiation, a compromise finally began to ______ from the discussions between both sides.
questions.explanation: Weeks of negotiation ending in a compromise means something gradually came into view, which is what 'emerge' describes. 'Vanish' reverses that, and neither purchasing nor rehearsing is something a compromise can do.

questions.prompt: The new safety procedures proved highly ______, reducing workplace injuries by almost half.
questions.explanation: Halving injuries is evidence that the procedures worked, which is what 'effective' means. The other three describe properties a set of procedures could technically have, but none of them would be demonstrated by a drop in injuries.

questions.prompt: Analysts were surprised by the sharp ______ in fuel consumption following the new tax.
questions.explanation: A tax on fuel would reduce how much is used, and 'decrease' names that fall. The other options are things that cannot be 'in fuel consumption' at all.

questions.prompt: He felt deeply ______ of his behaviour and apologised to everyone the following morning.
questions.explanation: The apology tells you he judged his own behaviour badly, which is what 'ashamed' means. 'Proud' and 'fond' would contradict the apology, and someone unaware of their behaviour would have no reason to apologise for it.

questions.prompt: The report contradicts several findings published in the ______ study by the same research team.
questions.explanation: A report can only contradict findings that already exist, so the study must be an earlier one — 'previous'. The other three are adjectives that cannot sensibly describe a research study here.

questions.prompt: The government was criticised for responding slowly to the housing ______ in the northern cities.
questions.explanation: Something a government is criticised for responding slowly to must be a serious problem, which 'crisis' names. None of the others is something that would require a government response.

questions.prompt: The festival was designed to ______ visitors from outside the region during the quiet winter months.
questions.explanation: A festival planned for a quiet season exists to bring people in, which is what 'attract' means. You cannot memorise, translate or inherit visitors.

questions.prompt: The lawyer argued that suspicion alone was not sufficient ______ of any wrongdoing by her client.
questions.explanation: Setting suspicion against what is 'sufficient' points at evidence, which is what 'proof' means. The others cannot be 'of wrongdoing'.

questions.prompt: A single careless remark can ______ an evening that everyone else had been enjoying.
questions.explanation: The contrast with everyone else enjoying it shows the remark ruins the evening, which is what 'spoil' means. Measuring, translating or inheriting an evening makes no sense.

questions.prompt: What began as an ______ Tuesday turned into the most memorable day of her career.
questions.explanation: 'Turned into the most memorable day' sets up a contrast with something unremarkable, which is what 'ordinary' means. A Tuesday cannot be imaginary, electrical or edible in any ordinary reading.

questions.prompt: Engineers developed a small ______ that measures air quality and sends readings to a phone.
questions.explanation: Something engineers develop that measures and transmits is a piece of equipment — a 'device'. None of the other options can measure anything.

questions.prompt: Disagreements inevitably ______ when two departments are given responsibility for the same budget.
questions.explanation: Overlapping responsibility causes disagreements to come about, which 'arise' describes. Disagreements are not things that rehearse, translate or inherit.

questions.prompt: The decision to close every branch at once was a ______ move that surprised the industry.
questions.explanation: Closing every branch at once is drastic and risky, and it surprised people — that is a 'bold' move. The other adjectives cannot describe a business decision.

questions.prompt: The charity worked for years to ______ relationships with donors in several different countries.
questions.explanation: Years of work on relationships means developing them carefully over time, which is what 'cultivate' means here. 'Abolish' would end them, and relationships are not memorised or translated.

questions.prompt: A single ______ at the figures was enough to tell her something had gone badly wrong.
questions.explanation: Something that takes only a moment and is done 'at the figures' is a quick look — a 'glance'. The other three cannot be directed at figures.

questions.prompt: The nurse cleaned the ______ carefully before applying a fresh bandage to his arm.
questions.explanation: Something cleaned before a bandage is applied is an injury, which 'wound' names. Nothing else listed can be bandaged.

questions.prompt: There has been a ______ change in how people book holidays since the pandemic ended.
questions.explanation: A change worth reporting since a major event is a large and striking one, which 'dramatic' describes. A change cannot be edible, audible or alphabetical here.

questions.prompt: Fewer than twenty students attended the final ______ of what had been a popular course.
questions.explanation: Something students attend as part of a course is a teaching session — a 'lecture'. None of the other options is something a course consists of.

questions.prompt: Doctors advised waiting until the swelling had begun to ______ before attempting any further treatment.
questions.explanation: You wait for swelling to go down before treating further, and 'subside' means to decrease. Swelling cannot rehearse, inherit or translate.

questions.prompt: Planners tend to ______ how long large infrastructure projects will actually take to complete.
